lines.text: From brass gears to thinking machines: five generations of computers, the systems and languages that run them, and the rise of artificial intelligence.
It begins with Charles Babbage, an English mathematician who dreamed of machines that could calculate, store numbers and follow a program.
Ada Lovelace studied his designs and wrote what is often called the first computer program. She saw that such machines could handle far more than numbers.
In 1822 Babbage designed his Difference Engine to print tables of numbers. He never finished it, but one built from his plans in 1991 worked.
His bigger dream, the Analytical Engine, had a store, a mill and punched cards for programs. It was never built, yet it was a modern computer in outline.
A century later Alan Turing described a machine that defined what computers can do. In wartime he helped break Enigma, and later asked whether machines can think.
In Berlin in 1941, Konrad Zuse finished the Z3, built from telephone relays. It is widely counted as the first working programmable digital computer.
Meanwhile British codebreakers built Colossus to read German messages. Using vacuum tubes, it was the first programmable electronic computer, and it stayed secret for decades.
Across the Atlantic, IBM and Harvard built the Mark One, a huge electromechanical calculator fed by long tapes of instructions. Grace Hopper was among its programmers.
In 1946 ENIAC filled a room with seventeen thousand vacuum tubes, calculating artillery tables for the US Army. Six women programmed it by rewiring it by hand.
At the end of 1947, Bell Labs built the first working transistor, a tiny switch that would one day replace the vacuum tube in every machine.
In 1948 the Manchester Baby ran a program held in its own electronic memory, the way every computer has worked ever since.
At Cambridge, EDSAC gave scientists a regular computing service. Its team wrote the first programming textbook and shared a library of subroutines.
Programmers soon stopped writing raw numbers. Assembly language gave each machine instruction a short readable name, and it is still used today.
UNIVAC One was built for business, with the Census Bureau as its first customer. In 1952 it famously predicted a presidential election on live television.
The IBM 650 was the first computer made in large numbers, almost two thousand of them. Many universities got their very first computer this way.
In the summer of 1956, a workshop at Dartmouth College gave a new field its name: artificial intelligence.
A year later IBM released Fortran, so scientists could write formulas instead of machine code. Nearly seventy years on, it still runs weather models.
Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron learned to tell simple shapes apart by adjusting its weights. It is the ancestor of today's neural networks.
ALGOL, designed by a European and American committee, was rarely used commercially, but its structure shaped Pascal, C and almost every language after.
John McCarthy created LISP for AI research. It gave programmers garbage collection and code written as data, and it is still alive today.
Also in 1958, Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit, many parts made together on one piece of semiconductor. The chip was born.
The PDP-1 was small enough for one person to sit at. At MIT it gave rise to hacker culture and Spacewar, one of the first video games.
The IBM 1401 took over payroll and billing from rooms of punched-card machines. For a while it was the most common computer in the world.
Its scientific cousin, the transistor-based IBM 7090, was faster and far more reliable. NASA used it to plan and track the Mercury and Gemini flights.
COBOL was written to read like English for business. It still keeps a large share of the world's banking and government records.
In 1964 IBM bet the company on System 360, a family of machines that all ran the same software. The bet paid off, and its programs still run today.
That same year Dartmouth made BASIC so every student could program. It later came built into nearly every home computer of the eighties.
In Norway, Simula invented classes, objects and inheritance, ideas that grew into Smalltalk, C plus plus and Java.
ELIZA played a therapist by turning your words back into questions. It understood nothing, yet people confided in it anyway.
Kenneth Iverson's APL worked on whole arrays at once, using special symbols. It is famously terse and still used in finance.
Shakey was the first mobile robot that could plan its own actions. Its project gave us methods still used in route finding today.
Logo taught children to program with a turtle that drew lines on the screen, all to help them learn mathematics.
Multics tried bold ideas in sharing and security. When Bell Labs left the project, two of its engineers set out to build something simpler.
The PDP-11 became the most popular minicomputer, with around six hundred thousand sold. Unix grew up on it, and C was written for it.
Niklaus Wirth's Pascal taught a generation to write well-structured code, and Apple wrote its early Lisa and Mac software in it.
In 1971 the Intel 4004 put a whole processor on a chip the size of a fingernail. The microprocessor had arrived, and the fourth generation with it.
That was the answer from Bell Labs: Unix, by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie. Its ideas live on in Linux, macOS, iOS and Android.
To build Unix, Dennis Ritchie wrote C, small and fast. Nearly every operating system still rests on it, and most languages borrowed its style.
Prolog let programmers state facts and rules and leave the computer to work out answers. It became a favourite of early AI.
At Xerox PARC, Smalltalk made everything an object, and its windows and live programming shaped the graphical interface.
PARC's Alto had a screen, a mouse and windows in 1973. It was never sold widely, but Apple and Microsoft learned from it.
Gary Kildall's CP M ran early microcomputers with floppy disks, until MS-DOS borrowed its ideas and pushed it aside.
At IBM, SQL gave people a way to ask questions of databases. It became the standard, and almost every business uses it.
The Cray One supercomputer was shaped like a letter C with a bench around its base, and it crunched numbers for labs and weather services.
At MIT, Scheme distilled Lisp into something small and elegant, ideal for teaching, and its ideas later shaped JavaScript.
The Altair 8800 was a hobby kit with only switches and lights. Bill Gates and Paul Allen wrote BASIC for it, and the personal computer age began.
In 1977 came the Apple Two, designed by Steve Wozniak, with colour graphics. The first spreadsheet made it a business machine too.
The same year Radio Shack sold the TRS-80 ready to use in thousands of ordinary shops. The personal computer had reached the public.
The US Department of Defense named its new safety-minded language Ada, after Lovelace. It still runs in aircraft, trains and spacecraft.
The Osborne One was the first portable to sell well, though it weighed about eleven kilos. Its maker collapsed after announcing the next model too soon.
Also in 1981, IBM launched its PC from off-the-shelf parts. Its open design was easy to clone, and today's PCs still descend from it.
Inside it ran MS-DOS, which Microsoft had bought and licensed to IBM. Every compatible PC booted into it for a decade, and it made Microsoft's fortune.
In Britain, the cheap ZX Spectrum with its rubber keys sold more than five million, and a generation learned to program on it.
Japan launched a ten-year push for a fifth generation of reasoning machines. It alarmed rivals into funding AI, but its computers found no market.
The Commodore 64 became the best-selling single computer model of all time, the first machine for countless programmers and game makers.
Richard Stallman began GNU, a free replacement for Unix that anyone could copy and change. With Linux it later became a complete system.
In 1984 Apple launched the Mac with a famous Super Bowl advert, bringing the mouse and windows to a mass market.
Its system software made icons and windows familiar to millions, though it was eventually replaced by a Unix-based successor.
Objective-C added Smalltalk-style messages to C. Through NeXT it became the language of Mac OS X and the first iPhone apps.
Cyc set out to write down, by hand, all the common sense people take for granted. Running for over forty years, it is a symbol of rule-based AI.
In 1985 the Amiga offered colour graphics, stereo sound and true multitasking, years ahead of most rivals, and artists and gamers loved it.
At Bell Labs, Bjarne Stroustrup added objects to C without losing speed. C plus plus now runs browsers, games and trading systems.
IBM and Microsoft wrote OS 2 together as a successor to DOS. Then they fell out, Microsoft chose Windows, and OS 2 retreated to banks and cash machines.
Larry Wall's Perl, the duct tape of the internet, ruled text processing and early web scripts through the nineties.
Steve Jobs's black NeXT cube sold poorly, but the first web browser was written on one, and its software became the base of macOS and iOS.
Haskell, designed by academics, was purely functional, with lazy evaluation and strong types that inspired many later languages.
Guido van Rossum started Python as a holiday project. Built for readable code, it became the main language of data science and machine learning.
Visual Basic let people build Windows programs by dragging and dropping, and brought millions of newcomers into programming.
That same year a student, Linus Torvalds, started Linux as a hobby. Built by thousands, it now runs most servers and every top supercomputer.
Windows 3.1 was the first Windows to be widely used, with TrueType fonts and steadier multitasking, selling in the tens of millions.
IBM's black ThinkPad, with its red pointing stick and sturdy keyboard, became the business traveller's laptop, and some even flew into space.
In 1993 Nvidia was founded to make graphics chips for games. Nobody guessed those chips would one day power artificial intelligence.
From Brazil came Lua, a tiny scripting language so easy to embed that games like World of Warcraft and Roblox use it.
Two professors in New Zealand wrote R for statistics and charts, now used by scientists, analysts and journalists.
FreeBSD carried on the Berkeley branch of Unix, and parts of it ended up inside the PlayStation and Apple's systems.
In 1995 Sun launched Java, promising code that runs anywhere. It became the language of enterprise servers and Android apps.
Rasmus Lerdorf wrote PHP for his own home page. It went on to power much of the dynamic web, from WordPress to Wikipedia.
Windows 95 arrived with the Start button, the taskbar and a huge launch, setting the look of Windows for decades.
Netscape built JavaScript to make web pages interactive. Today it runs in every browser, and on servers too.
BeOS was a fast multimedia system that Apple nearly bought. Instead its maker ran out of money and sold it to Palm.
Yukihiro Matsumoto designed Ruby to make programmers happy, and Ruby on Rails made it the language of web start-ups.
In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match, the first machine to do so.
On phones, Symbian powered Nokia as it led the market through the 2000s, until Android and the iPhone overtook it.
The colourful, see-through iMac dropped the floppy drive, embraced USB and the internet, and brought Apple back from the edge.
Nvidia's GeForce 256 was sold as the first GPU. Its descendants now train most of the world's AI.
In 2001 Apple released Mac OS X, built on NeXT's software and Unix, with a stable core and the Dock.
Windows XP brought home and business Windows together on one solid core, and stayed in use for well over a decade.
Microsoft answered Java with C sharp, led by Anders Hejlsberg. It grew into an open language for business software and Unity games.
Windows Vista had a new look but was criticised for slowness and endless security pop-ups, and it was soon replaced.
With CUDA, Nvidia let anyone program its graphics chips for general work. A graphics card became a cheap supercomputer, and the fifth generation took shape.
Also in 2007, Apple's iPhone put a full web browser and a multi-touch screen in a pocket, and phones became computers.
Its system, later called iOS, opened to outside apps a year on and created the app economy.
From MIT came Scratch, where learners snap coloured blocks together to make games. Schools around the world use it.
Steve Jobs pulled the MacBook Air from a paper envelope on stage, and slim laptops everywhere followed its lead.
IBM's Roadrunner, with chips borrowed from the PlayStation 3, was the first supercomputer to pass a quadrillion calculations a second.
Google gave Android, built on Linux, to phone makers for free. It became the most used operating system in the world.
Palm's webOS treated apps as cards you could swipe between. It failed on phones but found a second life in LG's televisions.
Windows 7 was quicker and simpler than Vista, and many people kept it for years, even after the updates stopped.
Google's Go was simple, fast to build and good at doing many things at once. It became the language of cloud tools like Docker.
In 2010 the iPad made tablets popular at last, after many earlier attempts had failed.
Microsoft's Windows Phone had bright tiles instead of icons, but never won enough apps or users, and Microsoft gave it up.
IBM's Watson beat two of the greatest Jeopardy champions in 2011. Turning it into a business, especially in medicine, proved much harder.
JetBrains released Kotlin, which runs on Java's platform. Google later made it a preferred language for Android apps.
Siri arrived on the iPhone 4S and put a talking assistant in millions of pockets, years before chatbots.
Rust began as one programmer's project and grew up at Mozilla, promising memory safety without slowing down. It is now inside the Linux kernel.
The Raspberry Pi put a whole computer on a small board for about the price of a textbook, made to help schools teach computing.
Google built ChromeOS around its browser. It starts quickly, updates itself, and fills many classrooms.
In 2012 AlexNet won a picture-recognition contest by a wide margin, trained on graphics chips. The deep learning boom had begun.
Microsoft added types to JavaScript with TypeScript, so big projects could catch mistakes early. It became the default for large web apps.
Microsoft's Cortana, named after a Halo character, came to phones and Windows 10 but never caught its rivals, and was later retired.
In 2014 Apple surprised developers with Swift, the replacement for Objective-C and now the main language for its apps.
Amazon's Alexa arrived inside the Echo speaker and put a talking computer into millions of kitchens and living rooms.
Google built its own chip just for neural networks, the Tensor Processing Unit, and put it to work in its data centres.
Windows 10 came as a free upgrade and ran on more than a billion devices, updated as a service.
AlphaGo mastered Go, a game experts thought was a decade out of reach. Its win over Lee Sedol in 2016 convinced millions that modern AI was real.
Google gave away TensorFlow, its library for building neural networks, putting deep learning in any programmer's hands.
That year OpenAI was founded as a non-profit research lab. It would go on to make the GPT models and ChatGPT.
In 2016 Microsoft's Tay chatbot learned from Twitter users, who taught it to post offensive messages. It was switched off within a day.
Google Assistant could hold a two-way conversation and reached more than a billion devices, before Gemini replaced it.
Elon Musk's Neuralink began work on a brain implant. In 2024 its first patient moved a cursor by thought alone.
In 2017 Google researchers introduced the Transformer, a design built on attention. It underlies nearly every large language model today.
DeepMind's AlphaFold predicted the shape of proteins from their sequence, a fifty-year problem, and gave its results to every scientist free.
IBM showed Q System One, the first quantum computer built as a complete product for business, sealed in a glass cube.
OpenAI's GPT-2 wrote text so convincing that the full model was held back at first, for fear it might be misused.
Google's Sycamore chip finished in minutes a task said to take supercomputers thousands of years, a claim called quantum supremacy.
GPT-3 showed that a large enough model can learn new tasks from just a few examples, and it became the base of ChatGPT's first model.
In Japan, Fugaku topped the world's supercomputer rankings and helped model the spread of COVID-19.
Apple's own M1 chip was faster than the Intel chips it replaced and used far less power, proving Arm could run full computers.
OpenAI's DALL-E drew pictures from written descriptions, and later versions made those pictures strikingly realistic.
GitHub Copilot began suggesting the next lines of code as programmers typed, the first AI coding tool to be widely used.
Windows 11 arrived with a centred taskbar, rounded windows and stricter hardware rules.
In 2022 Frontier, at Oak Ridge, became the first supercomputer to pass a quintillion calculations a second, the exascale era.
Nvidia's H100 chip became the most sought after hardware on Earth for training large language models.
Midjourney's painterly images, made by typing a description into a chat, spread across social media and sparked a fierce debate about AI and art.
Stable Diffusion released its model to the public, so anyone with a home graphics card could make images from words.
Then, at the end of 2022, ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in about two months and set off the race for AI assistants.
Meta's Llama models were released for anyone to download and build on, and became the base of many others.
Anthropic launched Claude, a family of language models and a chatbot also widely used for writing software.
Google answered with Bard, later renamed Gemini after the family of models behind it.
From China, DeepSeek's R1 model, said to be trained at a fraction of the usual cost, topped app charts and shook technology shares.
And in 2024 Google's Willow chip showed errors falling as more qubits were added, a key step towards useful quantum computers.
From Babbage's gears to machines that talk, and the next generation is already being built.
